title: Introduction attributes the whole parametric-vs-closure gap to the representation and explicitly rules out "the fit" — the paper's own measurement gives the objective the larger share
quoted_text:
The contribution is not that this can happen; it is a characterisation of
\emph{when} it happens, and a demonstration, through a chain of controls, that
the failure is a property of the flexible representation rather than of the data,
the fit, or the optimiser: on the same trajectory, a direct two-parameter fit
pins the conductance to about six per cent, while the estimates distilled from
the closure scatter across a factor of two and all but one of them fall outside
the short stretch of the trade-off the likelihood tolerates.
why_wrong: This is the one place in the manuscript where the compounded 6%-vs-40% contrast is presented flatly as a representation effect. The matched-objective control decomposes that gap as objective ~3.2x (6.2 -> 19.7%) and representation ~2.1x (19.7 -> 40.9%), so the objective — which is a property of the fitting criterion, not of the representation — owns the majority. The sentence not only omits that decomposition, it affirmatively excludes "the fit" from the list of things that could be responsible, which is the bucket the objective falls into (it is neither the data nor the optimiser nor the representation). The paper's own Results section states the opposite and commits to a rule this sentence breaks: line 1515-1518 reads "The representation is not innocent, but it owns about two-fifths of the gap on a log scale, less than the objective's share and not all of it, and we quote the twofold figure rather than the sixfold one wherever the two arms are compared." The abstract (245-248), Contribution 4 (373-377), the Discussion (1892-1894) and the Conclusion (1932-1935) all carry the qualification; the Introduction — the first place a reader meets the thesis — does not.
evidence: results/identifiability/parametric_matched_objective_summary.csv, gCa_true=2.0: chi2 rel_sd=0.0621, sse_full rel_sd=0.1974. Closure traj-train spread from results/identifiability/symbolic_domain_comparison.csv: 0.6718/1.6446 = 40.9%. Ratios 19.7/6.2 = 3.2 and 40.9/19.7 = 2.1; on a log scale the objective is 61% of the gap and the representation 39%. claims.yaml, closure-induced-nonidentifiability scope: "DECOMPOSITION, and this is the licensed one: objective ~3.2x (6.2 -> 19.7%), representation ~2.1x (19.7 -> 40.9%). Quote the ~2x figure for the representation, NEVER the ~6-7x ratio, which is objective and representation compounded." main.tex:1515-1518 states the same rule in the paper's own voice.
_a: paper/main.tex lines 1-420: preamble, byline, abstract, Introduction, Contributions (plus the first Related Work paragraph)

_v.reasoning: Confirmed verbatim at paper/main.tex:312-319. The sentence attributes the failure to "the flexible representation rather than of the data, the fit, or the optimiser". The paper's own Methods name the three differing things as "Representation, objective and optimiser" (main.tex:857-859), so "the fit" is the slot the objective occupies, and the Results measure that the objective owns the LARGER share: main.tex:1512-1517 reads "Descending a voltage-dominated objective ... accounts for about a threefold inflation on its own. The closure's forty per cent sits a further twofold above that. ... it owns about two-fifths of the gap on a log scale, less than the objective's share ... and we quote the twofold figure rather than the sixfold one wherever the two arms are compared." Line 313-319 compares the two arms (six per cent vs a factor-of-two scatter) and carries no such qualification, so it breaks the rule the paper sets for itself. The inconsistency is internal to the Introduction: Contribution 4 at main.tex:373-377 says "We do not attribute all of that to the representation, because the two arms also differ in objective ... the objective accounts for about a threefold inflation and the representation for a further twofold" — 58 lines after the sentence that rules the fit out. git log -L313,319:paper/main.tex shows "the fit, or the optimiser" is a leftover from the retired FALSE thesis (310855c: "the failure is a property of the data rather than of the fit or the optimiser"); a38745f moved "the data" into the exclusion list and inserted "the flexible representation" without revisiting the trailing list, and 03cf53b rewrote only the colon clause. The isomorphic defect was found and fixed at the two other sites in earlier rounds — paper/audit-2026-08-21-triage.json contains "Conclusion presents the closure as the sole surviving explanation and never mentions the measured objective/optimiser contribution" (MAJOR) and the Discussion counterpart (MINOR), and both now carry concessions at main.tex:1891-1894 and 1932-1935, with the abstract carrying it at 245-248. Neither audit file contains any entry touching 313-319 (no occurrence of "fit, or the optimiser"), so this site was missed rather than deliberately declined; it is not on the settled list. Secondary checks that do NOT undercut the finding: "scatter across a factor of two" is accurate (SymbolicAHatRangeTrajTrain raw min=1.241 max=2.816 per metrics_map.yaml:1255-1261, a 2.27x span), and the sentence quotes no forbidden six/sevenfold ratio — the defect is the affirmative exclusion of "the fit" plus the absent decomposition, not a wrong number.
_v.corrected_location: paper/main.tex:313-319 (the defective clause is the exclusion list on lines 315-316: "rather than of the data, / the fit, or the optimiser")
_v.corrected_fix: Drop "the fit" from the exclusion list and carry the measured split into the Introduction, matching the concessions already present in the abstract (245-248), Contribution 4 (373-377), Discussion (1891-1894) and Conclusion (1932-1935). For example, replace lines 313-319 with: "The contribution is not that this can happen; it is a characterisation of \emph{when} it happens, and a demonstration, through a chain of controls, that the failure is a property of the flexible representation rather than of the data: on the same trajectory, a direct two-parameter fit pins the conductance to about six per cent, while the estimates distilled from the closure scatter across a factor of two and all but one of them fall outside the short stretch of the trade-off the likelihood tolerates. The two arms also differ in objective, and we measure that rather than assume it away: the objective accounts for about a threefold inflation of the parametric spread and the representation for a further twofold." Keep the "% claim: closure-induced-nonidentifiability" anchor on line 312; no \val macros or numok literals are introduced, since "six per cent", "a factor of two", "threefold" and "twofold" are the same word-form quantities already used at 371-377 and 1509-1517.

title: Table 3 caption says the second column's spread widens toward the top row; the printed spread narrows
quoted_text:
the spread in the second column widens as the calcium signal
  shrinks toward the top row, and that is information
  loss rather than misfit.
why_wrong: The second column is $\hat g_{Ca}$ (parametric), printed as mean ± 1 SD. Reading the table bottom-to-top the printed ± values are 0.120 (gCaHi 4.0), 0.130 (gCaMain 2.0), 0.084 (gCaMid 1.0), 0.065 (gCaPhys 0.4). The spread a reader can actually see in that column gets *smaller* toward the top row, not larger. Only the RELATIVE spread widens (2.9% -> 6.2% -> 8.1% -> 14.9%), which is what the body prose at line 1533 correctly says ("its relative spread widening from $2.9$ to $14.9$ per cent"). The caption drops the word "relative" and therefore asserts the opposite of what its own table shows. A reader who checks the caption against the column finds a direct contradiction.
evidence: Table body, paper/main.tex:1626-1629, renders \valParamFitGcaHatPointFourMeanStd=0.438 \pm 0.065, \valParamFitGcaHatOneMeanStd=1.043 \pm 0.084, \valParamFitGcaHatTwoMeanStd=2.092 \pm 0.130, \valParamFitGcaHatFourMeanStd=4.105 \pm 0.120 (paper/generated/metrics.tex). Recomputed from results/identifiability/parametric_fit.csv: SD 0.0651 at gCa=0.4, 0.0839 at 1.0, 0.1300 at 2.0, 0.1199 at 4.0; relative 14.9%, 8.1%, 6.2%, 2.9%. Body prose at paper/main.tex:1533 says "relative spread" and carries the numok "% numok: relative spreads, results/identifiability/parametric_fit.csv".
_a: paper/main.tex lines 1300-1760: symbolic recovery, parametric reference, retrain control, Tables 3 and 4

_v.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The text is present verbatim right now at paper/main.tex:1603-1605, inside the Table 3 (\label{tab:parametric}) caption: "...so each fit sits at the / known noise floor; the spread in the second column widens as the calcium signal / shrinks toward the top row, and that is information / loss rather than misfit."

The second column is $\hat g_{Ca}$ (parametric). The same caption fixes its format two sentences earlier at line 1597: "The $\hat g_{Ca}$ column is mean $\pm$ 1 SD over the seeds". So "the spread in the second column" is the printed absolute SD, and the printed absolute SDs, read bottom-to-top (paper/main.tex:1626-1629 -> paper/generated/metrics.tex:662,583,645,627), are 4.105 ± 0.120, 2.092 ± 0.130, 1.043 ± 0.084, 0.438 ± 0.065. Toward the top row that spread NARROWS (0.130 -> 0.084 -> 0.065), and it is not even monotone over the full sweep (0.120 at gCaHi vs 0.130 at gCaMain). I recomputed from results/identifiability/parametric_fit.csv (n=5 each): SD 0.0651 / 0.0841 / 0.1300 / 0.1198 at gCa = 0.4 / 1.0 / 2.0 / 4.0; relative 14.9 / 8.1 / 6.2 / 2.9 per cent. Only the RELATIVE spread widens toward the top row, monotonically.

The body prose gets this right and the caption does not, which is what makes it a defect rather than loose phrasing: paper/main.tex:1533 says "its / relative spread widening from $2.9$ to $14.9$ per cent across the sweep % numok: relative spreads, results/identifiability/parametric_fit.csv". The caption drops "relative" while pointing the reader at a column it has just told them is an absolute SD, so a reader who checks the caption against the column sees the opposite of what the caption asserts.

Two possible defences, both of which I checked and rejected. (1) "Second column" might mean the second DATA column, i.e. rel. SE ($\valCondRelSeGcaPointFourMean$ = 0.269 at gCaPhys vs $\valCondRelSeGcaTwoMean$ = 0.067 at gCaMain), which does widen toward the top. But the table's column spec is \begin{tabular}{lcccc} with header "True $g_{Ca}$ & $\hat g_{Ca}$ (parametric) & rel.\ SE ...", so the second column is plainly $\hat g_{Ca}$; and rel. SE is discussed separately in its own clause immediately before ("Relative standard errors come from the Fisher information in log parameters"), so reading "second column" as rel. SE would make that clause redundant and leave rel. SE named twice by two different labels. (2) "The spread" might inherit "relative" from the preceding rel.-SE clause, but the intervening $\chi^2$/point clause breaks that chain, and the phrase explicitly re-anchors to a column.

This is not on the settled list, is not something a mechanical checker can see (no number is quoted in the sentence, so Law I is satisfied and the numbers checker has nothing to flag), and it is a genuine sentence-vs-evidence disagreement. Severity MINOR is right: the substantive point — graceful degradation as the calcium signal shrinks — is correct and correctly stated elsewhere; only this caption clause misdescribes it.
_v.corrected_location: paper/main.tex:1603 (Table 3 caption, \label{tab:parametric}); compare correct body wording at paper/main.tex:1533
_v.corrected_fix: Insert the missing qualifier so the caption matches both its own column and the body prose. Change line 1603 from "the spread in the second column widens as the calcium signal" to "the \emph{relative} spread in the second column widens as the calcium signal". If a reader should also be kept from expecting the absolute SD to grow, the fuller form is: "the second column's relative spread widens as the calcium signal shrinks toward the top row --- even as its absolute SD narrows --- and that is information loss rather than misfit." No number is introduced either way, so no \val macro and no "% numok:" comment is required; the quantitative version of the same statement already lives at paper/main.tex:1533 with its numok pointing at results/identifiability/parametric_fit.csv.

title: Window-sweep gaps are judged against the forecast-window seed spread, not the common-eval spread the sweep is scored on
quoted_text:
The twenty- and thirty-millisecond
windows are indistinguishable ($\valWindowAblCommonEvalVRmseTwenty$ and
$\valWindowAblCommonEvalVRmseThirty$\,mV, a gap well inside the
$\pm\valUdeForecastVRmseStd$\,mV five-seed spread at the centre point), while the
why_wrong: The paragraph opens by stating the sweep is "scored on the shared unseen window $t>\Tcommon$\,ms" (line 1241-1242), and 0.225/0.236 are indeed common_eval_V_rmse values. But the yardstick \valUdeForecastVRmseStd (0.028) is the five-seed SD of the FORECAST-window V RMSE (t>30), a different metric on a different interval. The matching quantity exists and is already a macro: \valCommonEvalVRmseFullStd = 0.037 (CommonEvalVRmseFull = 0.266 +/- 0.037, same t>50 window, same 5 seeds, same metric). Using 0.028 understates the correct yardstick by ~24%. The paper's own metrics_map.yaml:461-463 warns about exactly this pair -- "Not the same quantity as UdeForecastVRmse (0.245 +/- 0.028): that is the forecast window (t > 30) over 5 seeds, this is the common-eval window (t > 50) at one seed. Do not conflate them." No conclusion changes (0.011 is well inside 0.037 too), so this is a wrong-macro defect, not a wrong-number one.
evidence: generated/metrics.tex:59 \valUdeForecastVRmseStd = 0.028 (forecast window); generated/metrics.tex:1168 \valCommonEvalVRmseFullStd = 0.037 (t>50, n=5). results/ablation_window.csv common_eval_V_rmse = 1.5586/0.22524/0.23608/0.36717/0.41772 for t_train_end 15/20/30/40/50 -- these are the numbers being compared. metrics_map.yaml:461-463 explicitly separates the two quantities.
_a: paper/main.tex lines 940–1300: forecasting section, voltage-only section, the three ablations (gCa / window / noise), Table 2 (tab:forecast) and the figure captions in that span (fig:node-vs-ude, fig:ude-overview, fig:bars, fig:voltage-only, fig:gca)

_v.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The quoted text is present verbatim at paper/main.tex:1246-1249, inside the paragraph that opens (line 1241-1242) with "The training-window sweep, scored on the shared unseen window $t>\Tcommon$\,ms" where \Tcommon = 50 (main.tex:64).

The three sweep numbers are common-eval quantities: metrics_map.yaml WindowAblCommonEvalVRmseTwenty/Thirty read column `common_eval_V_rmse` from results/ablation_window.csv (0.22523666920122537 at t_train_end=20, 0.23608373353853263 at 30), i.e. V RMSE on t > 50, single seed 1111.

The yardstick they are held against is not that quantity. generated/metrics.tex:59 gives \valUdeForecastVRmseStd = 0.028, and metrics_map.yaml:144-152 defines UdeForecastVRmse from metrics_baseline_multiseed.csv with filter {model: UDE, observed: full, window: forecast, metric: V_rmse}, mean 0.245 std 0.028, its own note saying "358 forecast points (t > 30 ms)". So the sentence calibrates a t>50 gap against a t>30 spread.

The exactly matching statistic exists and is already a macro: generated/metrics.tex:1159/1168 \valCommonEvalVRmseFull = 0.266 +/- 0.037 and \valCommonEvalVRmseFullStd = 0.037, defined at metrics_map.yaml:1695-1702 as {model: UDE, observed: full, window: common_eval, metric: V_rmse} aggregated over 5 seeds — same model, same 5 seeds, same metric, same t>50 interval as the sweep is scored on. The single-seed centre value 0.236 sits inside that 0.266 +/- 0.037, so the two are consistent computations of the same thing.

The repo itself flags the hazard at metrics_map.yaml:461-463: "Not the same quantity as UdeForecastVRmse (0.245 +/- 0.028): that is the forecast window (t > 30) over 5 seeds, this is the common-eval window (t > 50) at one seed. Do not conflate them." The competing in-repo instruction that appears to license the 0.028 comparator (metrics_map.yaml:424-426, "the +/-0.028 seed spread at t_train=30 (UdeForecastVRmse) is comparable to the 20-30 and 30-40 gaps") dates to the original draft commit 310855c, whereas CommonEvalVRmseFull only entered at a38745f — so this reads as a stale comparator that was never updated when the matching common-eval multiseed statistic arrived, not as a settled decision. It is also not on the settled list.

Scope and severity: this is a wrong-macro defect, not a wrong-number one. The direction is conservative (0.028 understates the correct spread by ~24%), so nothing downstream flips — 0.011 is well inside 0.037, and the later "several times that spread" for 0.367/0.418 still reads as 3.5x and 4.9x under 0.037. The mechanical checkers cannot catch it: \valUdeForecastVRmseStd is a legitimate macro tracing to a real CSV cell, so Law I passes; only reading the sentence against the interval it is scored on exposes the mismatch. Hence MINOR, and confined to this one sentence — the parallel caption at main.tex:2112-2113 says "several times the five-seed spread at the centre point" with no number attached and is unaffected, as is the unrelated correct use of \valUdeForecastVRmseStd at main.tex:1020, which is genuinely describing forecast-window seed variability.
_v.corrected_location: paper/main.tex:1249 (the token `\valUdeForecastVRmseStd` in the parenthetical spanning lines 1247-1249)
_v.corrected_fix: Swap the yardstick macro to the one measured on the interval the sweep is scored on, and name the window so the reader can see they match. Replace `$\pm\valUdeForecastVRmseStd$\,mV five-seed spread at the centre point` with `$\pm\valCommonEvalVRmseFullStd$\,mV five-seed spread of the same common-eval metric at the centre point`. Optionally cite the pair it comes from, `$\valCommonEvalVRmseFull$\,mV`, already used at main.tex:1166, so the provenance is visible in prose. No other edit is needed: the following clause's "several times that spread" remains true under 0.037 (the 40 ms and 50 ms rises are 3.5x and 4.9x), the figure caption at main.tex:2112-2113 quotes no number, and the separate use of \valUdeForecastVRmseStd at main.tex:1020 is correct there and must be left alone. Also update the stale guidance at paper/metrics_map.yaml:424-426 to point at CommonEvalVRmseFullStd for the window axis, so the map stops recommending the mismatched comparator.

title: Three preamble provenance pointers into src/metrics.jl are stale by eleven lines and land on comment text, not on the values they claim to cite
quoted_text:
\newcommand{\Ttube}{10}        % rollout tube threshold, mV            src/metrics.jl:81
\newcommand{\Rcap}{70}         % rollout cap_ms                        src/metrics.jl:82
...
\newcommand{\Rsus}{1.0}        % rollout sustained_ms                  src/metrics.jl:82
why_wrong: Law I lets a preamble \newcommand stand in for a \val macro only because the source comment names the line an auditor can check. src/metrics.jl:81 is a bare "#" and :82 is the first line of the RIGHT-CENSORING prose block; the actual definitions (thresh_mv = 10.0, sustained_ms = 1.0, cap_ms = 70.0) sit at lines 92-93, inside the rollout_horizon signature. An auditor who follows either pointer lands on real code comments and finds nothing to verify. check_provenance_refs.py cannot catch this class — its own docstring says "It cannot tell a pointer that is in range but points at the wrong thing", and it only WARNs when the cited line is blank or a bare delimiter, which neither of these is. The neighbouring pointers in the same block (\Vthresh -> metrics.jl:31, \SpikeSep -> :31, \SpikeTol -> :54) are all exact, and every src/hh_core.jl pointer in the preamble is exact, so this trio is isolated drift rather than a convention.
evidence: src/metrics.jl:81 = "#"; :82 = "#  RIGHT-CENSORING.  A run that never breaches is censored, and it is censored at"; :92 = "function rollout_horizon(Vp, Vt, t; thresh_mv = 10.0, t_start = 30.0,"; :93 = "                         sustained_ms = 1.0, cap_ms = 70.0)". Running scripts/check_provenance_refs.py emits 13 WARNs, none of them for these three pointers.

I tried to refute this and could not — the drift is present in the current tree and is provable from git history.

paper/main.tex:68  `\newcommand{\Ttube}{10}        % rollout tube threshold, mV            src/metrics.jl:81`
paper/main.tex:69  `\newcommand{\Rcap}{70}         % rollout cap_ms                        src/metrics.jl:82`
paper/main.tex:72  `\newcommand{\Rsus}{1.0}        % rollout sustained_ms                  src/metrics.jl:82`

src/metrics.jl as it stands today:
  81 | `#`
  82 | `#  RIGHT-CENSORING.  A run that never breaches is censored, and it is censored at`
  92 | `function rollout_horizon(Vp, Vt, t; thresh_mv = 10.0, t_start = 30.0,`
  93 | `                         sustained_ms = 1.0, cap_ms = 70.0)`

So :81 is a bare comment marker with no content at all, and :82 is a prose line that does not name cap_ms (that word first appears on :83) and never mentions sustained_ms. All three cited lines carry none of the three values. The real definitions are on 92-93.

PROVENANCE OF THE DRIFT (this is what makes it certain rather than plausible): `git show 7ec58a0^:src/metrics.jl` gives
  81 | `function rollout_horizon(Vp, Vt, t; thresh_mv = 10.0, t_start = 30.0,`
  82 | `                         sustained_ms = 1.0, cap_ms = 70.0)`
The pointers were exactly right before commit 7ec58a0 ("Work the 81-finding referee report"), which inserted the 11-line RIGHT-CENSORING comment block (`git log -S "RIGHT-CENSORING"` returns that single commit). The function moved 81->92, 82->93; the three preamble comments were not moved with it. The auditor's "stale by eleven lines" is numerically exact, not a guess.

CHECKS ON THE REFUTATION SIDE, all of which failed to clear it:
- Not on the settled list. Nothing in the settled items covers preamble source-comment pointers.
- Not caught by any checker. I ran scripts/check_provenance_refs.py: it reports 160 pointers, 13 WARNs, and none of them are for main.tex:68, :69, or :72 — exactly as the auditor states. Its in-range/wrong-target blind spot is real: it only WARNs when the cited line is blank or `end`, and `#` plus a prose line are neither. (It does WARN on main.tex:73 -> metrics.jl:167 'end', a separate already-visible pointer, not this trio.)
- Not a house convention of pointing at the docstring rather than the code. title: SINDy wrong-sign result is restated in the Discussion without its single-seed qualifier; it holds for 2 of 5 seeds
why_wrong: As written this reads as a property of the sparse regression across the study, and it is offered as one of "Three independent instances" alongside two five-seed results. §results-symbolic states it correctly and narrowly: "At the representative seed the physical $Vs^2$ term is even fitted with the \emph{wrong sign}" (main.tex:1396-1398). In the data only seeds 1111 (-1.469) and 5555 (-7.963) are negative; 2222 (+4.783), 3333 (+1.275) and 4444 (+5.124) have the right sign. Given how scrupulously the paper tags every other single-seed number ("single seed", "$\dagger$~Single seed", "One run per point"), dropping the qualifier here overstates the instance.
evidence: results/symbolic/sindy_coefficients.csv, row `V*s^2`: -1.4692, 4.7834, 1.2752, 5.1237, -7.9635 for seeds 1111/2222/3333/4444/5555 at gCa=2.0. Compare main.tex:1396-1398.
_a: paper/main.tex lines 1760-2130 — Discussion, Limitations, Conclusion, Data and Code Availability, Appendices A-C and their figure captions

_v.reasoning: Confirmed from current contents. paper/main.tex:1826-1828 reads "sparse regression attains a high $R^2$ against the true current while fitting the physical $Vs^2$ term --- the one that carries the conductance --- with the wrong sign;" with no seed qualifier, offered as instance (i) of "Three independent instances" whose siblings ARE scoped ("five seeds reach..."; "the retrain holds forecast accuracy on the representative seed"). The Results section states it narrowly at main.tex:1395-1396: "At the representative seed the physical $Vs^2$ term is even fitted with the \emph{wrong sign}". Data: results/symbolic/sindy_coefficients.csv row `V*s^2` at gCa=2.0 gives -1.4692 (1111), +4.7834 (2222), +1.2752 (3333), +5.1237 (4444), -7.9635 (5555) against a true +2.0 (claims.yaml:477 confirms the truth is 2*V*s^2 - 240*s^2), so the sign is wrong at only 2 of 5 seeds. All five seeds have high r2_sindy_true (0.988/0.964/0.995/0.980/0.852), so the high-R^2 half is general while the wrong-sign half is not. The paper's own ledger anchors the sign failure to one run (metrics_map.yaml:583-584: "V·s² carries coefficient −1.469 at seed 1111 — THE WRONG SIGN against a true +2.0"), and every other "wrong sign" in the manuscript is scoped (main.tex:1234-1235 "hull domain, single seed"; main.tex:1496-1497 "single seed"). Line 1828 is the only unqualified occurrence, so it reads as a property of sparse regression across the study rather than of the representative seed. Not on the settled list; not catchable by the eight mechanical checkers since it is a scope-vs-evidence mismatch, not a macro or bare literal. Note claims.yaml:869-870 carries the same unqualified phrasing in the claim's scope, so the ledger propagates rather than rescues the gap. Severity MINOR: the transferable point survives, only its stated generality does not.
_v.corrected_fix: Restore the seed scope so the Discussion matches Sec. results-symbolic and the ledger, e.g. change lines 1826-1828 to: "instances make the point here: sparse regression attains a high $R^2$ against the true current at every seed while fitting the physical $Vs^2$ term --- the one that carries the conductance --- with the wrong sign at the representative seed;". This adds no new numeral, so Law I needs no new macro or "% numok:" and the checkers stay green. If a count is preferred over "at the representative seed", write "at two of the five seeds" with a same-line "% numok: sign count of the V*s^2 row, results/symbolic/sindy_coefficients.csv (seeds 1111, 5555 negative against a true +2.0)". _v.reasoning:
Confirmed present and wrong, though the auditor's framing needs tightening.

paper/main.tex:2091-2094 currently reads: "the two-stage trainer records / whether the BFGS polish succeeded, but that flag is written out only for the / aggressive-retrain and neural-ODE parity runs; for the baseline and ablation / sweep it is discarded, so a silent degradation to the Adam result would not be / visible in those tables."

There is a third run family that writes the flag out. gca_sweep_5seed.jl:71-73 pushes `bfgs_ok = r.bfgs_ok` into log_rows and line 79 does `CSV.write(RUNLOG, DataFrame(log_rows))` with RUNLOG = results/gca_sweep_5seed/run_log.csv (line 33). That file is on disk with header `gCa,seed,final_loss,bfgs_ok,status` and twelve rows, all `true,ok`. This is exactly the same standard the sentence already applies to the neural-ODE parity runs, whose flag also lives in a run log (results/node_parity/run_log.csv), not in a reported table — so by the sentence's own criterion the five-seed conductance sweep counts as "written out". The word "only" is therefore false.

Where the auditor overreaches: the paper's five-seed conductance sweep is a MIXTURE, not a single script's output. scripts/summarize_gca_sweep.py's docstring is explicit — gCa=2.0 (all five seeds) and the seed-1111 cells at gCa in {0.4,1.0,4.0} are re-used from results/metrics_all.csv, whose header is `model,observed,gCa,noise_level,t_train_end,seed,window,metric,value` (no bfgs_ok); only seeds 2222-5555 at those three gCa values come from gca_sweep_5seed.jl. title: eq:chisq defines sigma_i from SD of the noisy data; the code uses SD of the clean signal
why_wrong: Line 735 defines $u(t)=(V,m,h,n,p,s)$ as "the noisy data", and eq:chisq uses that same $u_i(t)$ in the numerator of the residual. So $\mathrm{SD}(u_i)$ reads as the standard deviation of the noisy channel. The code computes sigma from the CLEAN trajectory: identifiability_parametric.jl:167 `sigma = B_NOISE .* std(data_clean, dims = 2)`, matching gen_noisy_data (src/hh_core.jl:169) which scales the OU path by `noise_level .* std(data_clean, dims=2)`. The paper's own preamble comment for \LossShareV (main.tex:134-138) is explicit that the shares are "Computed from the clean gCa=2.0 trajectory". The numerical difference is ~0.02% (sqrt(1+0.02^2)), so nothing downstream moves; the defect is that the symbol as written does not name the quantity the code uses, in the one equation whose whole point is that sigma_i is the *known* noise magnitude. Writing $\mathrm{SD}$ of the clean channel (or introducing separate notation for the clean trajectory) would fix it.
_a: paper/main.tex lines 700-940 — Methods: TikZ schematic, NODE baseline, UDE + eq:loss, symbolic recovery, parametric reference + eq:chisq, training protocol. Cross-checked against src/experiment.jl (make_ude_loss, make_ca_network, train_two_stage, run_experiment, run_node_baseline, solve_aligned), src/hh_core.jl (make_hh_advanced, gen_noisy_data, SCALE, make_split), src/metrics.jl (ICa_rmse_norm), identifiability_parametric.jl (make_objective, fit_params, STARTS, PART 3 profiles, PART 4 Fisher), parametric_matched_objective.jl, objective3_symbolic.jl, and results/*.csv.

_v.reasoning:
Confirmed from current contents; I could not refute it. paper/main.tex:735 binds the symbol once and unambiguously — "$u(t)=(V,m,h,n,p,s)$ for the noisy data" — and grep over lines 700-900 shows no redefinition of $u$ and no symbol anywhere in the paper for the clean trajectory. eq:chisq then reuses that same $u_i(t)$ in the residual numerator (paper/main.tex:836) and defines the weight as "\sigma_i = \NoisePct\,\%\times \mathrm{SD}(u_i)." (paper/main.tex:838). The only available reading is 2% of the SD of the realized NOISY channel.

The code uses the clean channel. identifiability_parametric.jl:167 `sigma = B_NOISE .* std(data_clean, dims = 2)`, under the comment on :166 "Known per-channel noise SD, as constructed by gen_noisy_data", which matches src/hh_core.jl:169 `return data_clean .+ noise_level .* std(data_clean, dims = 2) .* ou`. The script's own header at identifiability_parametric.jl:92-93 spells it out: "sigma_i the KNOWN per-channel noise standard deviation (noise_level * std of that channel's clean signal — exactly how gen_noisy_data builds it)". The paper's preamble comment agrees against the equation: main.tex:151-152 "sigma_i = 0.02 x channel SD of the clean gCa=2.0 trajectory (src/hh_core.jl:169)".

Beyond the symbol mismatch there is an internal tension five lines below the equation. main.tex:843 asserts "Here $\sigma_i$ is the \emph{known} noise magnitude of each channel, since we generated it." SD of the realized noisy sample is a statistic estimated from the data, not a known generative constant; SD of the clean channel is known because the clean trajectory is deterministic given the parameters. Since eq:chisq is the one objective the paper treats as a log-likelihood carrying a chi-square threshold, having its sigma read as data-estimated undercuts exactly the property the equation is introduced for.

Severity is correctly NIT: the gap is sqrt(1+0.02^2) = 1.0002, about 0.02%, so no reported number moves, and the data-generation prose at main.tex:655-656 ("scaled to \NoisePct\,\% of that channel's own standard deviation", said of the trajectory being noised) is itself correct. The defect is confined to the single equation line. It is not on the settled list, and no mechanical checker compares a symbol's binding against the quantity the code computes.
_v.corrected_fix: Make the equation name the clean channel. Cheapest edit that keeps Law I intact: introduce a clean-trajectory symbol at the existing binding site (main.tex:735), e.g. "Writing $u(t)=(V,m,h,n,p,s)$ for the noisy data, $u^{\ast}(t)$ for the clean trajectory it was built from, and $\hat u(t;\theta)$ for the solver's output", then change line 838 to "\sigma_i = \NoisePct\,\%\times \mathrm{SD}(u^{\ast}_i)." Alternatively, if adding notation is unwelcome, leave the formula and amend the sentence at main.tex:843 to state the generative definition outright, e.g. "Here $\sigma_i$ is the \emph{known} noise magnitude of each channel, \NoisePct\,\% of the clean channel's standard deviation, since we generated it that way (src/hh_core.jl:169)." The first option is preferable because it fixes the equation itself rather than glossing it. No \val macro or CSV is affected; \NoisePct is unchanged and the preamble comment at main.tex:151-152 already documents the clean-trajectory basis.
